title: How an independent hotel should write an about page
metaTitle: How an independent hotel writes about
excerpt: Name the people a guest will meet and the hours they cover. Skip the origin story unless it changes whether someone checks dates.
alt: A hand holding a blue pen over wireframe sketches, with a mug and a closed notebook nearby, drafting who actually stands behind a stay.
caption: The pen is on the sketch, not on a slogan. An about page should name the rota. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: Who should a hotel about page name?
faqs.answer: The people a guest will meet: whoever locks the door, cooks breakfast, or answers a late arrival. Give each a name, a role, and the hours that role covers. If the team is two people, say so. Small is a fact, not a flaw to costume.

faqs.question: When does a founding story belong?
faqs.answer: When it explains a constraint the guest will meet, such as a stair that cannot be widened or a kitchen that can only serve a set breakfast. A tale about taste or travel can sit lower, or it can stay off the page. Open with the names.

faqs.question: What should the about page ask the reader to do?
faqs.answer: Check dates, after the names have done their work. Repeat the limit that most often changes a booking, such as stairs or a minimum stay. A long contact form here teaches that an ordinary night requires a correspondence.

markdown:
An independent hotel about page should prove that specific people stand behind the stay. Name who does the work, and say why a traveler comparing three properties should care. Skip the origin myth unless it changes the decision to check dates.

Google's helpful-content guidance treats "who" as a trust question: a visitor should be able to tell who is responsible for what they are reading, and the page should show experience that comes from being there. An about page is that answer for a hotel. A crest, a Latin line, or a fable about a grandmother's suitcase does not substitute for a name and a role.

## Who is on the property

Start with the person a guest will actually meet. The owner who lives upstairs. The manager who locks the door. The cook who is there for breakfast and not for dinner. A night contact, if the night contact is real. Give each one a name, a role, and the hours that role covers.

A portrait helps when it is the person, in the building, in clothes they wear to work. A portrait hurts when it is a lifestyle photograph of hands on a linen napkin and no face. The traveler is deciding whether to sleep in your house. Faces are part of that decision. If someone does not want to be pictured, use their name and role anyway. Absence of a photograph is honest. A stock smile is not.

Say what each person decides. "Mara handles breakfast and the courtyard, and she is the one to tell if you need to leave before seven." That sentence does more than a paragraph about Mara's love of travel. Authority, in a small hotel, is operational. Who can move a room. Who cannot promise a late dinner. Who will answer if the taxi is late.

If the team is two people, say two people. Small is not a flaw to costume. A traveler comparing three stays is often hoping for small, and they need to know the smallness is staffed. "We are a family-run house" is fine if it is true and if you then name the family members who work there. The phrase alone is a genre, not a proof.

## Why this traveler cares

The reader is not your biographer. They are choosing a night. They care about the about page only where it changes the risk they feel. Risk, for this buyer, sounds like: Will someone be there if the train is late? Is the house a stage set or a place with judgment? Will a promise made by email be kept by the person at the desk?

Write toward those worries. "Someone is on site from 7 a.m. to 11 p.m., and the phone we give you reaches a person who can come downstairs." That is why they should care. "Our story began in 2014 with a dream" does not touch the worry. It asks for patience the traveler is spending in the other tabs.

You can still be warm. Warmth is naming the habit of the house: bags held if they arrive early, a note when the street market will be loud, a refusal to book the lively room for a guest who asked for quiet. Those are reasons to care because they predict the stay. Character, on this page, is a pattern of decisions, not a list of adjectives.

If you have a point of view that changes the booking, put it high. Adults only. No televisions. One seating at breakfast. A building that is old and sounds like it. The about page is a fair place for the point of view, as long as the dates are still one click away. A point of view that is only aesthetic, "we believe in slow mornings," needs a concrete partner or it will not survive the comparison.

## When an origin story earns its place

An origin earns its place when it explains a constraint the guest will meet. The house was a bakery, so the front room has no window and we use it as a library, not a bedroom. The owner kept the narrow stair because widening it would have broken the listing, so every room above the first floor is a stair room. The cook started here because the kitchen is four burners, which is why breakfast is a set plate and not a menu.

That kind of origin changes the decision to check dates. It tells the traveler what they are walking into, and why the place did not become a different place. It is useful.

An origin that does not earn its place is the voyage of taste. A trip to Kyoto. A love of linen. A manifesto about hosting. These can be true and still be irrelevant to a Friday-night choice. If you want them, put them under the facts, in a short passage, after the names and the hours. Do not open with them. The first screen of the about page is still a decision screen.

Read the origin aloud and then ask: would this sentence change which room I book, or whether I book at all? If the answer is no, the sentence can live in a dinner conversation. It does not need the page.

## What to cut from the founder essay

Cut the adjectives you would be embarrassed to say to a guest's face. Passionate. Bespoke. World-class. Nestled. Cut the claim that you are "not like other hotels" unless the next sentence is the specific difference, such as no front desk after eleven, or a single shared table.

Cut awards unless you can say what they were for, in a few words, and you are willing to leave them off if they are obscure to your guest. A badge row is not an about page. A sentence is sometimes enough, and sometimes the honest choice is silence.

Cut the group photograph where nobody is identified. Cut the timeline of renovations that reads like a permit history. Keep one renovation fact if it explains the room: new beds in March, the street-facing windows resealed, the bathroom in the small double still original and therefore small.

Cut a letter from the founder that never mentions the guest's decision. If you keep a letter, make it short enough to finish, sign it with the name the guest will meet, and end on how to check dates. A letter that ends on "we cannot wait to welcome you" has not told them how to become a guest.

The essay's job is finished when a skeptical person could tell who runs the house tonight. If your draft cannot pass that test without the adjectives, the draft is still a costume.

## Names, roles, and the desk

Put names where they can be checked against the stay. The confirmation note should match the about page. If "Jonas handles arrivals," Jonas should not be a surprise brand while a different person opens the door with no introduction. Alignment here is a small operational task and a large trust task.

Roles should be current. Update the page when someone leaves, in the same week, not at the next redesign. An about page with a former manager is worse than a short page, because the guest will ask for a person who cannot appear. Keep the roster short enough that you will maintain it.

If the owner is not on site, do not imply that they are. "Owned by Ana, run day to day by Luis and Priya" is a clear structure. Guests are not owed the owner's life story. They are owed the truth about who can solve a problem at 9 p.m.

The desk itself can be described as a place: where it is, that it is a table and not a counter, what is on it. This sounds minor. It tells a nervous arrival what to look for. Independent hotels often fail this in person, not only online, because the entrance is a hallway. The about page can prevent the three-minute panic.

## Hand the page back to the dates

The about page is not the last step. A traveler who now trusts the people still needs a night that exists. Close with check dates, in a sentence, not a billboard. "If the way we run the house fits, see whether your dates are open." Repeat the constraint that most often changes the booking, in one line, so they carry it into the checker: stairs, a minimum stay, breakfast that ends at 10.

Do not add a contact form that is longer than the biographies. Questions belong on the contact path. This page's action remains the dates. A form here teaches the wrong lesson, that booking is a correspondence, when for most nights it is not.

If you mention the building's limits again, keep them consistent with the room page. The about page is where people go to resolve doubt. A contradiction between "quiet house" here and "lively street" on the room page reopens every doubt you just closed. One description. Use it everywhere.

Invite a staff member to read their own paragraph and delete one line. The line they delete is usually the one a copywriter added to make them sound grand. Grand is not the goal. Recognizable is the goal.

## Where proof goes next

Names establish who. They do not yet show a hard decision about the room itself: a constraint, a choice, and the room as it stands. That belongs on a proof page. [How to show one true decision about the room](/blog/proof-pages-for-an-independent-hotel) is the next piece, because a pleasant biography can still leave the traveler unsure what they will sleep in.

If you want help deciding which sentences earn the page and which are the origin myth, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring the current about text and the names of the people on this week's rota. The gap between those two documents is the rewrite.
